claims.evidence: Cited from published literature.

claims.claim: Localized knockdowns of Drosophila ASCIZ using RNAi show mitotic defects.
claims.source: Drosophila ASCIZ knockouts die in early embryogenesis and localized knockdowns using RNAi show mitotic defects (Zaytseva et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature.

claims.claim: Mutant phenotypes in Drosophila, developing mouse B lymphocytes, and cultured cells are rescued by ectopic overexpression of LC8.
claims.source: Mutant phenotypes in Drosophila, developing mouse B lymphocytes, and cultured cells are rescued by ectopic overexpression of LC8, demonstrating that the observed defects of ASCIZ knockouts are due to ASCIZ regulation of LC8 expression (Goggolidou et al., 2014b; Jurado et al., 2012b; Zaytseva et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature.

claims.claim: The observed defects of ASCIZ knockouts are due to ASCIZ regulation of LC8 expression.
claims.source: Mutant phenotypes in Drosophila, developing mouse B lymphocytes, and cultured cells are rescued by ectopic overexpression of LC8, demonstrating that the observed defects of ASCIZ knockouts are due to ASCIZ regulation of LC8 expression (Goggolidou et al., 2014b; Jurado et al., 2012b; Zaytseva et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Inferred from rescue experiments cited from literature.

claims.claim: A conditional knockout of LC8 almost perfectly copies the corresponding phenotypes of ASCIZ knockouts in mouse B cell development and B cell lymphomagenesis.
claims.source: In addition, it has recently been shown that a conditional knockout of LC8 almost perfectly copies the corresponding phenotypes of ASCIZ knockouts in mouse B cell development and B cell lymphomagenesis (King et al., 2017; Wong et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature.

claims.claim: LC8 is a highly conserved 20.6 kDa protein homodimer (10.3 kDa monomer).
claims.source: LC8 is a highly conserved 20.6 kDa protein homodimer (10.3 kDa monomer) that facilitates self-association of its primarily disordered partners (Barbar, 2008; Barbar and Nyarko, 2014; Clark et al., 2015) (Figure 1a).
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature and shown in Figure 1a.

claims.claim: LC8 facilitates self-association of its primarily disordered partners.
claims.source: LC8 is a highly conserved 20.6 kDa protein homodimer (10.3 kDa monomer) that facilitates self-association of its primarily disordered partners (Barbar, 2008; Barbar and Nyarko, 2014; Clark et al., 2015) (Figure 1a).
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature.

claims.claim: LC8 binding is associated with a range of cellular processes, from cell division to apoptosis.
claims.source: LC8 binding is associated with a range of cellular processes, from cell division to apoptosis, underscoring LC8's essential role as a regulatory hub (Dunsch et al., 2012; Puthalakath et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature.

claims.claim: LC8 preferentially binds to a 10-amino acid motif in intrinsically disordered regions containing highly conserved TQT residues at positions 7–9.
claims.source: LC8 preferentially binds to a 10-amino acid motif in intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) containing highly conserved TQT residues at positions 7–9 (Barbar, 2008; Rapali et al., 2011b) (Figure 1b).
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature and shown in Figure 1b.

claims.claim: In complex with LC8, the otherwise intrinsically disordered motif adopts a ß-strand conformation.
claims.source: In complex with LC8, the otherwise intrinsically disordered motif adopts a ß-strand conformation (Benison et al., 2007; Liang et al., 1999) (Figure 1a,b).
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature and shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: The Q residue in the TQT motif is involved in interactions with both LC8 subunits in the dimer.
claims.source: Analysis of the 11 crystal structures of LC8 bound to short peptides containing the motif explains why the TQT residues are essential for binding: the Q is involved in interactions with both LC8 subunits in the dimer, while both T's are fully buried and thus evolutionarily constrained.
claims.evidence: Inferred from analysis of crystal structures.

claims.claim: Both T residues in the TQT motif are fully buried and thus evolutionarily constrained.
claims.source: Analysis of the 11 crystal structures of LC8 bound to short peptides containing the motif explains why the TQT residues are essential for binding: the Q is involved in interactions with both LC8 subunits in the dimer, while both T's are fully buried and thus evolutionarily constrained.
claims.evidence: Inferred from analysis of crystal structures.

claims.claim: TQT acts as the motif anchor while the other seven highly variable motif residues modulate affinity.
claims.source: In these interactions, TQT acts as the motif anchor while the other seven highly variable motif residues modulate affinity, as described in the anchored flexibility model of LC8 motif recognition (Clark et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature.

claims.claim: LC8 binds one motif in each of its two symmetrical binding grooves.
claims.source: LC8 binds one motif in each of its two symmetrical binding grooves (Figure 1a), creating an IDP duplex that serves as a bivalent scaffold.
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 1a and stated in text.

claims.claim: LC8 binding creates an IDP duplex that serves as a bivalent scaffold.
claims.source: LC8 binds one motif in each of its two symmetrical binding grooves (Figure 1a), creating an IDP duplex that serves as a bivalent scaffold.
claims.evidence: Stated in text and illustrated in Figure 1.

claims.claim: The IDP duplex scaffold aids in higher order complex assembly by promoting binding of other proteins, including additional LC8 dimers.
claims.source: This scaffold aids in higher order complex assembly by promoting binding of other proteins, including additional LC8 dimers (Figure 1c), and enhancing self-association and oligomerization processes that often involve coiled-coil formation (Hall et al., 2009; Kidane et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature and shown in Figure 1c.

claims.claim: The number of experimentally characterized LC8 partners has risen to more than 40.
claims.source: In recent years, the number of experimentally characterized LC8 partners has risen to more than 40, and prediction methods indicate that dozens more may specifically bind LC8 (Rapali et al., 2011b).
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature.

claims.claim: Prediction methods indicate that dozens more proteins may specifically bind LC8.
claims.source: In recent years, the number of experimentally characterized LC8 partners has risen to more than 40, and prediction methods indicate that dozens more may specifically bind LC8 (Rapali et al., 2011b).
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature.

claims.claim: Human ASCIZ contains 11 functional LC8 binding sites.
claims.source: Although some LC8 partners have multiple recognition motifs (Dunsch et al., 2012; Fejtova et al., 2009; Gupta et al., 2012; Stelter et al., 2007) (Nucleoporin Nup159 has 5, Chica and Bassoon each has 3), human ASCIZ contains 11 functional LC8 binding sites (Rapali et al., 2011a), the most by far of any partner protein identified to date.
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature.

claims.claim: Human ASCIZ has the most LC8 binding sites of any partner protein identified to date.
claims.source: Although some LC8 partners have multiple recognition motifs (Dunsch et al., 2012; Fejtova et al., 2009; Gupta et al., 2012; Stelter et al., 2007) (Nucleoporin Nup159 has 5, Chica and Bassoon each has 3), human ASCIZ contains 11 functional LC8 binding sites (Rapali et al., 2011a), the most by far of any partner protein identified to date.
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature and compared to other known partners.

claims.claim: The enrichment in LC8-binding sites is conserved throughout the animal kingdom.
claims.source: This enrichment in LC8-binding sites is conserved throughout the animal kingdom, underscoring the importance of multiple motifs in ASCIZ function (Figure 1d).
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 1d through sequence analysis of ASCIZ proteins from different species.

claims.claim: ASCIZ regulates LC8 transcription via a system of negative autoregulation.
claims.source: Cell culture transcription assays demonstrate that ASCIZ regulates LC8 transcription via a system of negative autoregulation, for which the mechanism is not well understood.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through cell culture transcription assays.

claims.claim: Disruption of the ASCIZ/LC8 interaction via mutation of the TQT sites results in an increased level of LC8 transcription.
claims.source: Disruption of the ASCIZ/LC8 interaction via mutation of the TQT sites results in an increased level of LC8 transcription, while overexpression of LC8 decreases transcription (Jurado et al., 2012a).
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature.

claims.claim: Overexpression of LC8 decreases ASCIZ transcription.
claims.source: Disruption of the ASCIZ/LC8 interaction via mutation of the TQT sites results in an increased level of LC8 transcription, while overexpression of LC8 decreases transcription (Jurado et al., 2012a).
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature.

claims.claim: ASCIZ acts as a sensor for cellular LC8 and regulates LC8 transcription levels according to cellular needs.
claims.source: This observation led to the hypothesis that ASCIZ acts as a sensor for cellular LC8 and regulates LC8 transcription levels according to cellular needs (Jurado et al., 2012a).
claims.evidence: Hypothesis cited from published literature.

claims.claim: LC8 expression levels vary among tissue types.
claims.source: As LC8 expression levels vary among tissue types (Chintapalli et al., 2007) and LC8 overexpression enhances the survival and proliferation of breast cancer cells in culture (Vadlamudi et al., 2004), regulation of LC8 levels is critical for cellular health and homeostasis.
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature.

claims.claim: LC8 overexpression enhances the survival and proliferation of breast cancer cells in culture.
claims.source: As LC8 expression levels vary among tissue types (Chintapalli et al., 2007) and LC8 overexpression enhances the survival and proliferation of breast cancer cells in culture (Vadlamudi et al., 2004), regulation of LC8 levels is critical for cellular health and homeostasis.
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature.

claims.claim: Regulation of LC8 levels is critical for cellular health and homeostasis.
claims.source: As LC8 expression levels vary among tissue types (Chintapalli et al., 2007) and LC8 overexpression enhances the survival and proliferation of breast cancer cells in culture (Vadlamudi et al., 2004), regulation of LC8 levels is critical for cellular health and homeostasis.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the cited effects of LC8 expression variation and overexpression.

claims.claim: The 45 kDa Drosophila ASCIZ protein is predicted to contain four Zn-finger motifs at the N-terminus followed by a 243-amino acid long region of intrinsic disorder.
claims.source: The 45 kDa Drosophila ASCIZ protein, dASCIZ, is predicted to contain four Zn-finger motifs at the N-terminus followed by a 243-amino acid long region of intrinsic disorder.
claims.evidence: Based on sequence predictions.

claims.claim: The disordered region of dASCIZ has six predicted LC8 recognition sites identified by a canonical TQT motif.
claims.source: The disordered region has six predicted LC8 recognition sites identified by a canonical TQT motif (Figure 2a, dark blue bars): QT1 (residues 251–262), QT2 (274–285), QT4 (323–334), QT5 (340–351), QT6 (354–365), and QT7 (374–385).
claims.evidence: Predicted from sequence and shown in Figure 2a.

claims.claim: QT3 (285–296) lacks the TQT residues but is identified experimentally as an LC8 recognition site.
claims.source: QT3 (285–296) lacks the TQT residues but is identified experimentally as an LC8 recognition site in this work (below).
claims.evidence: Identified experimentally through ITC and NMR in this study.

claims.claim: The dZnF domain (residues 1–156) is monomeric in solution with a molecular weight of 17.4 kDa.
claims.source: Sedimentation velocity analysis of the dZnF and dLBD (Figure 2b) indicates that each is a monomer in solution with molecular weights of 17.4 kDa and 18 kDa, respectively (theoretical MW 17.6 kDa and 17 kDa).
claims.evidence: Determined by sedimentation velocity analysis shown in Figure 2b.

claims.claim: The dLBD (residues 241–388) is monomeric in solution with a molecular weight of 18 kDa.
claims.source: Sedimentation velocity analysis of the dZnF and dLBD (Figure 2b) indicates that each is a monomer in solution with molecular weights of 17.4 kDa and 18 kDa, respectively (theoretical MW 17.6 kDa and 17 kDa).
claims.evidence: Determined by sedimentation velocity analysis shown in Figure 2b.

claims.claim: The CD spectrum of dZnF shows a large negative ellipticity at 208 nm and a small negative ellipticity at 222 nm indicative of a mix of alpha helices and loops.
claims.source: The CD spectrum of dZnF shows a large negative ellipticity at 208 nm and a small negative ellipticity at 222 nm (Figure 2c, red) indicative of a mix of alpha helices and loops, similar to CD spectra of other ZnF proteins (Ezomo et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: Measured by CD spectroscopy shown in Figure 2c and compared to literature.

claims.claim: The dLBD CD spectrum has a large negative ellipticity at 200 nm, indicating that it is primarily disordered.
claims.source: The dLBD CD spectrum has a large negative ellipticity at 200 nm, indicating that it is primarily disordered (Figure 2c, blue).
claims.evidence: Measured by CD spectroscopy shown in Figure 2c.

claims.claim: Backbone assignments for 90% of the 148 residues in dLBD were obtained from 5D NMR experiments.
claims.source: From 5D NMR experiments, backbone assignments for 90% of the 148 residues in dLBD were obtained (Figure 2d).
claims.evidence: Obtained from 5D NMR experiments shown in Figure 2d.

claims.claim: A high level of disorder in dLBD is revealed by the limited amide proton chemical shift dispersion in 15N HSQC spectra.
claims.source: A high level of disorder in dLBD is revealed by the limited amide proton chemical shift dispersion in 15N HSQC spectra (Figure 2d), and a lack of secondary structure preference is further supported by small ΔCα-ΔCβ chemical shift differences from random coil values (Figure 2e).
claims.evidence: Observed in NMR spectra shown in Figure 2d.

claims.claim: A lack of secondary structure preference in dLBD is supported by small ΔCα-ΔCβ chemical shift differences from random coil values.
claims.source: A high level of disorder in dLBD is revealed by the limited amide proton chemical shift dispersion in 15N HSQC spectra (Figure 2d), and a lack of secondary structure preference is further supported by small ΔCα-ΔCβ chemical shift differences from random coil values (Figure 2e).
claims.evidence: Measured by NMR and shown in Figure 2e.

claims.claim: R2/R1 values for dLBD range from 1.5 to 5.3 with an average of 3.3.
claims.source: R2/R1 values range from 1.5 to 5.3 with an average of 3.3 (Figure 2f).
claims.evidence: Measured by NMR relaxation experiments shown in Figure 2f.

claims.claim: Relatively higher R2/R1 values for residues 321–363 suggest motional restriction in this region of dLBD.
claims.source: Relatively higher R2/R1 values for residues 321–363 suggest motional restriction in this region.
claims.evidence: Inferred from NMR relaxation data shown in Figure 2f.

claims.claim: Heteronuclear NOE values measured at 10°C for dLBD are very low overall, with values ranging from −0.1 to 0.3.
claims.source: Heteronuclear NOE values measured at 10°C are very low overall, with values ranging from −0.1 to 0.3, but are also slightly higher for residues 321–363 (Figure 2g).
claims.evidence: Measured by NMR and shown in Figure 2g.

claims.claim: Heteronuclear NOE values are slightly higher for residues 321–363 in dLBD.
claims.source: Heteronuclear NOE values measured at 10°C are very low overall, with values ranging from −0.1 to 0.3, but are also slightly higher for residues 321–363 (Figure 2g).
claims.evidence: Measured by NMR and shown in Figure 2g.

claims.claim: The R2/R1 and heteronuclear NOE values imply that dLBD is highly flexible with slight motional restriction in its C-terminal half.
claims.source: Together, the R2/R1 and heteronuclear NOE values imply that dLBD is highly flexible with slight motional restriction in its C-terminal half.
claims.evidence: Inferred from NMR relaxation data in Figures 2f and 2g.

claims.claim: The C-terminal constructs QT4-6 and QT4-7 are slightly more ordered than N-terminal constructs QT1-3 and QT2-4.
claims.source: Circular dichroism demonstrates that the C-terminal constructs, QT4-6 and QT4-7, are slightly more ordered than N-terminal constructs, QT1-3 and QT2-4 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by CD spectroscopy shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claims.claim: The QT4-6 and QT4-7 constructs are more compact than the N-terminal constructs as shown by size-exclusion chromatography.
claims.source: Size-exclusion chromatography supports this result, as the QT4-6 and QT4-7 constructs elute later, indicating that they are more compact than the N-terminal constructs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by size-exclusion chromatography shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claims.claim: The full length dLBD binds LC8 with a dLBD:LC8 stoichiometry of 1:7 (two chains of dLBD for 7 LC8 dimers).
claims.source: The full length dLBD binds LC8 with a dLBD:LC8 stoichiometry of 1:7 (two chains of dLBD for 7 LC8 dimers) and an overall Kd of 1.4 μM (Figure 3a, Table 1), suggesting that an additional non-TQT ASCIZ site binds LC8.
claims.evidence: Measured by ITC shown in Figure 3a and Table 1.

claims.claim: The full length dLBD binds LC8 with an overall Kd of 1.4 μM.
claims.source: The full length dLBD binds LC8 with a dLBD:LC8 stoichiometry of 1:7 (two chains of dLBD for 7 LC8 dimers) and an overall Kd of 1.4 μM (Figure 3a, Table 1), suggesting that an additional non-TQT ASCIZ site binds LC8.
claims.evidence: Measured by ITC shown in Figure 3a and Table 1.

claims.claim: A TMT motif corresponding to residues 285–296 (designated QT3) is a plausible candidate for an additional non-TQT ASCIZ site that binds LC8.
claims.source: The full length dLBD binds LC8 with a dLBD:LC8 stoichiometry of 1:7 (two chains of dLBD for 7 LC8 dimers) and an overall Kd of 1.4 μM (Figure 3a, Table 1), suggesting that an additional non-TQT ASCIZ site binds LC8. A plausible candidate is a TMT motif corresponding to residues 285–296 (designated QT3 in Figure 3a).
claims.evidence: Inferred from ITC stoichiometry and sequence analysis.

claims.claim: QT1-3 and QT2-4 bind LC8 with a stoichiometry of 3, demonstrating that the TMT motif is the seventh LC8 recognition site.
claims.source: QT1-3 and QT2-4 contain the TMT binding motif, and both bind LC8 with a stoichiometry of 3, demonstrating that this TMT motif is the seventh LC8 recognition site (Figure 3b, Table 1).
claims.evidence: Measured by ITC shown in Figure 3b and Table 1.

claims.claim: Construct QT4-6 binds LC8 with a Kd of 1.0 μM, a slightly higher overall affinity than the full dLBD construct.
claims.source: Interestingly, construct QT4-6, containing recognition sites 4–6, binds LC8 with a Kd of 1.0 μM, a slightly higher overall affinity than the full dLBD construct.
claims.evidence: Measured by ITC shown in Figure 3b and Table 1.

claims.claim: QT4-7 binds LC8 with a 1.6 μM affinity and is slightly more entropically disfavored than either QT4-6 or dLBD.
claims.source: QT4-7, on the other hand, binds LC8 with a 1.6 μM affinity and is slightly more entropically disfavored than either QT4-6 or dLBD (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Measured by ITC shown in Table 1.

claims.claim: The overall Kd values of QT1-3, QT2-4, and QT4-7 are 2.4 μM, 4.1 μM, and 1.6 μM, respectively.
claims.source: The overall Kd values of QT1-3, QT2-4, and QT4-7, are 2.4 μM, 4.1 μM, and 1.6 μM, respectively.
claims.evidence: Measured by ITC shown in Table 1.

claims.claim: QT3p interaction with LC8 is not detected at 30 μM LC8.
claims.source: QT3p interaction with LC8 is not even detected at 30 μM LC8.
claims.evidence: Measured by ITC shown in Figure 3c.

claims.claim: The QT4-6 construct has a slightly higher binding affinity than the other constructs, while the QT4, QT5, and QT6 peptides display among the lowest affinity as individual peptides.
claims.source: Intriguingly, the QT4-6 construct has a slightly higher binding affinity than the other constructs, while the QT4, QT5, and QT6 peptides display among the lowest affinity as individual peptides.
claims.evidence: Measured by ITC shown in Figure 3 and Tables 1-2.

claims.claim: Positive cooperativity enhances LC8 binding to neighboring recognition motifs in ASCIZ.
claims.source: Intriguingly, the QT4-6 construct has a slightly higher binding affinity than the other constructs, while the QT4, QT5, and QT6 peptides display among the lowest affinity as individual peptides. These results indicate that positive cooperativity enhances LC8 binding to neighboring recognition motifs.
claims.evidence: Inferred from comparison of ITC data for constructs versus individual peptides.

claims.claim: At a saturating concentration of LC8 (1:10 ratio), a high occupancy complex whose size (7.5 s) approximately corresponds to a fully bound complex (197 kDa) is clearly evident.
claims.source: At a saturating concentration of LC8 (1:10 ratio), a high occupancy complex whose size (7.5 s) approximately corresponds to a fully bound complex (197 kDa) is clearly evident.
claims.evidence: Observed by AUC shown in Figure 4a.

claims.claim: At saturating LC8 concentration, a low stoichiometry complex (5 s, approx. 114 kDa) is even more highly populated than the high occupancy complex.
claims.source: Contrary to expectations, a low stoichiometry complex (5 s, approx. 114 kDa) is even more highly populated.
claims.evidence: Observed by AUC shown in Figure 4a.

claims.claim: The molecular weight of the low occupancy complex corresponds roughly to a 1:3 complex.
claims.source: A high frictional ratio (f/f0 ~ 1.6) indicates an elongated complex, and the molecular weight of this low occupancy complex corresponds roughly to a 1:3 complex, although its broadness, and the approximate nature of the molecular weight determination, indicate that multiple species are present.
claims.evidence: Calculated from AUC data shown in Figure 4a.

claims.claim: The low occupancy peak is a heterogeneous mixture of 1:2, 1:3 and 1:4 complexes.
claims.source: It is likely that the low occupancy peak, which is roughly twice the intensity of the high occupancy peak, is a heterogeneous mixture of 1:2, 1:3 and 1:4 complexes.
claims.evidence: Inferred from AUC data shown in Figure 4a.

claims.claim: Low occupancy complexes are favored, relative to higher occupancy complexes, even in samples having a large excess of LC8.
claims.source: In summary, while high occupancy complexes are evident in AUC profiles, consistent with the ITC results, these complexes are in equilibrium with many smaller sub-saturated species, the most populated of which is a mixture of 1:2-1:4 complexes of dLBD:LC8. The low occupancy complexes are favored, relative to higher occupancy complexes, even in samples having a large excess of LC8.
claims.evidence: Observed by AUC shown in Figure 4a.

claims.claim: SAXS data indicate a monodisperse sample of dLBD:LC8 complexes with Dmax = 240 Å and a molecular weight of roughly 110 kDa.
claims.source: The distance distribution function suggests a moderately compact structure for dLBD:LC8 complexes, with Dmax = 240 Å, and a molecular weight of roughly 110 kDa, confirming the presence of an unresolved mixture of dLBD:LC8 complexes with stoichiometries ranging from 1:2-1:4 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b).
claims.evidence: Measured by SAXS shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: A Kratky plot of the scattering data indicates that the dLBD:LC8 complex is a mix of globular domains and intrinsically disordered chains.
claims.source: Additionally, a Kratky plot of the scattering data indicates that the dLBD:LC8 complex is a mix of globular domains and intrinsically disordered chains, consistent with low occupancy complex structures (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
claims.evidence: Measured by SAXS shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1c.

claims.claim: Native gel electrophoresis titration of dLBD with LC8 corroborates the presence of a mixture of complexes.
claims.source: Native gel electrophoresis titration of dLBD with LC8 corroborates the presence of a mixture of complexes (Figure 4b).
claims.evidence: Observed by native gel electrophoresis shown in Figure 4b.

claims.claim: Unbound LC8 is clearly visible at ratios ≥ 1:4, indicating that a pool of free LC8 accumulates even at conditions well below LC8 saturation of dLBD.
claims.source: Unbound LC8 is clearly visible at ratios ≥ 1:4, indicating that a pool of free LC8 accumulates even at conditions well below LC8 saturation of dLBD.
claims.evidence: Observed by native gel electrophoresis shown in Figure 4b.

claims.claim: The gel titration data for dLBD and hLBD suggest that hLBD:LC8 complexes form a dynamic ensemble with varying levels of LC8 occupancy in which lower occupancy forms are favored.
claims.source: Together the gel titration data for dLBD and hLBD suggest that hLBD:LC8 complexes form a dynamic ensemble with varying levels of LC8 occupancy in which lower occupancy forms are favored.
claims.evidence: Inferred from native gel electrophoresis data shown in Figures 4b and 4c.

claims.claim: A low occupancy intermediate (LMW) is clearly evident at the lowest molar ratio of 1:3 and persists at the same elution volume even at the highest molar ratios.
claims.source: A low occupancy intermediate, labeled LMW, is clearly evident at the lowest molar ratio of 1:3, and persists at the same elution volume even at the highest molar ratios.
claims.evidence: Observed by size-exclusion chromatography shown in Figure 4d.

claims.claim: A low occupancy form of the hLBD:LC8 complex is favored even with a large excess of LC8.
claims.source: Taken together, the data in Figure 4 are consistent with the explanation that a low occupancy form of the hLBD:LC8 complex is favored even with a large excess of LC8.
claims.evidence: Inferred from size-exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 4d.

claims.claim: Both Drosophila and human LBD exhibit dynamic behavior, suggesting it is a conserved feature of the ASCIZ:LC8 interaction.
claims.source: Both Drosophila and human LBD exhibit this dynamic behavior, suggesting it is a conserved feature of the ASCIZ:LC8 interaction.
claims.evidence: Inferred from comparison of data for dLBD and hLBD shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: In negative stain images of dLBD:LC8 and hLBD:LC8 complexes, the vast majority of complex species appear dissociated on the grid.
claims.source: In contrast, despite the similar overall affinity (Nup159-LC8 Kd = 2.9 μM) (Nyarko et al., 2013), in negative stain images of dLBD:LC8 and hLBD:LC8 complexes, the vast majority of complex species appear dissociated on the grid (Figure 5a, arrow heads).
claims.evidence: Observed by electron microscopy shown in Figure 5a.

claims.claim: A few observable complexes of dLBD:LC8 and hLBD:LC8 could be clearly resolved from raw micrographs, identified as linear stacks of punctate densities.
claims.source: However, a few observable complexes could be clearly resolved from raw micrographs, identified as linear stacks of punctate densities, akin of beads on a string (Figure 5a, squares), similar to images of Nup159 bound to LC8 (Stelter et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: Observed by electron microscopy shown in Figure 5a.

claims.claim: The vast majority of dLBD:LC8 and hLBD:LC8 complexes observed by EM appeared to be of low LC8 occupancy.
claims.source: Furthermore, although dLBD contains seven and hLBD 11 LC8 binding sites, the vast majority of complexes observed by EM appeared to be of low LC8 occupancy.
claims.evidence: Observed by electron microscopy shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Only low-occupancy oligomers with 2–4 LC8 dimers (2mer – 4mers) were successfully averaged in 2D projection averages.
claims.source: Representative 2D projection averages of (top) dLBD:LC8 oligomers and (bottom) hLBD:LC8 oligomers. Only low-occupancy oligomers with 2–4 LC8 dimers (2mer – 4mers) were successfully averaged.
claims.evidence: Observed by electron microscopy and 2D classification shown in Figure 5b.

claims.claim: Higher-occupancy oligomers were identified in raw micrographs but were not averaged due to low population and/or high degree of conformational flexibility.
claims.source: Higher-occupancy oligomers were identified in raw micrographs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), but were not averaged due to low population and/or high degree of conformational flexibility.
claims.evidence: Observed by electron microscopy shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Both dLBD:LC8 and hLBD:LC8 complexes form an ensemble of structures, displaying an exponential distribution with low-occupancy states (i.e. 2–4 stacked LC8 dimers) being most abundant.
claims.source: Both dLBD:LC8 and hLBD:LC8 complexes form an ensemble of structures, displaying an exponential distribution with low-occupancy states (i.e. 2–4 stacked LC8 dimers) being most abundant (Figure 5c,d).
claims.evidence: Observed by electron microscopy and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5c,d.

claims.claim: High-occupancy and fully-formed complexes of dLBD:LC8 (1:7 ratio) could be identified from the raw single particle images.
claims.source: Although uncommon, high-occupancy and fully-formed complexes of dLBD:LC8 (1:7 ratio) could be identified from the raw single particle images (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), further confirming the stoichiometry obtained by our ITC studies.
claims.evidence: Observed by electron microscopy shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: For the hLBD:LC8 dataset, complexes containing as many as 7–9 LC8 dimers could be distinguished from the single particle image data.
claims.source: For the hLBD:LC8 dataset, complexes containing as many as 7–9 LC8 dimers could be distinguished from the single particle image data, while higher-order complexes containing 10–11 LC8 dimers were either not distinguishable or were simply absent under the limiting concentrations required for negative stain EM specimen preparation.
claims.evidence: Observed by electron microscopy shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The remarkable similarity in distribution of oligomeric species formed by dLBD and hLBD suggests that a conserved mechanism of negative cooperativity is used by ASCIZ to regulate the formation and distribution of higher-order LC8 assemblies.
claims.source: Nevertheless, the remarkable similarity in distribution of oligomeric species formed by dLBD and hLBD, obtained under similar binding conditions, is consistent with the nearly equivalent overall LC8 affinity determined by ITC, and suggests that a conserved mechanism of negative cooperativity is used by ASCIZ to regulate the formation and distribution of higher-order LC8 assemblies.
claims.evidence: Inferred from comparison of EM and ITC data for dLBD and hLBD.

claims.claim: At a molar ratio of 1:5, less than 10% of the original peak intensity remains at all seven LC8 binding sites in dLBD.
claims.source: At a molar ratio of 1:5, less than 10% of the original peak intensity remains at all seven LC8 binding sites.
claims.evidence: Measured by NMR titration shown in Figure 6a.

results.result: Drosophila ASCIZ (dASCIZ) contains a structured N-terminal zinc finger domain and a long intrinsically disordered C-terminal domain (dLBD) with seven LC8 recognition motifs. The dLBD is highly flexible with slight motional restriction in its C-terminal half, and both domains are monomeric in solution.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C53 provide comprehensive structural characterization of dASCIZ using multiple complementary techniques (AUC, CD, NMR). The data consistently demonstrate that dLBD is intrinsically disordered with seven LC8 binding sites (including the non-canonical QT3 site), and both domains are monomeric. NMR relaxation data (R2/R1, heteronuclear NOE) support the conclusion of high flexibility with modest C-terminal restriction.

results.result: ITC experiments reveal that dLBD binds LC8 with a 1:7 stoichiometry and overall Kd of 1.4 μM. A seventh non-canonical TMT motif (QT3) was identified. Comparison of multi-motif constructs versus individual peptides demonstrates positive cooperativity among neighboring LC8 binding sites, with the QT4-6 construct showing the highest affinity.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C63 present a systematic ITC characterization of LC8 binding to dLBD constructs and peptides. The identification of QT3 as a functional binding site despite lacking TQT is validated by stoichiometry measurements. The evidence for positive cooperativity is compelling: QT4-6 construct binds with higher affinity (1.0 μM) than individual QT4, QT5, QT6 peptides (14-20 μM), demonstrating enhancement from neighboring motifs.

results.result: At saturating LC8 concentrations, both dLBD and hLBD form dynamic ensembles favoring low occupancy complexes (1:2-1:4 stoichiometry) over fully saturated complexes. This behavior is conserved between Drosophila and human ASCIZ and is supported by AUC, SAXS, native gel electrophoresis, and size-exclusion chromatography.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C77 demonstrate negative cooperativity through multiple orthogonal techniques. AUC shows a more populated low occupancy peak (5s, ~114 kDa) than high occupancy peak (7.5s, ~197 kDa) at 1:10 ratio. SAXS confirms MW ~110 kDa consistent with 1:2-1:4 complexes. Native gels show free LC8 accumulation at ratios ≥1:4, indicating saturation resistance. The conservation in both dLBD and hLBD strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: Negative stain electron microscopy reveals that dLBD:LC8 and hLBD:LC8 complexes form heterogeneous assemblies with an exponential distribution favoring low-occupancy states (2-4 LC8 dimers). The vast majority of complexes appear dissociated or in low occupancy states, with high-occupancy complexes being rare but detectable.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C86 provide direct visualization of the dynamic ensemble. The EM data show sparse, heterogeneous structures contrasting with stable Nup159:LC8 complexes. 2D classification successfully averaged only 2-4mer complexes due to conformational flexibility. Statistical analysis of ~2300 dLBD and ~1000 hLBD particles shows exponential distribution with 2-4mers most abundant. The similarity between dLBD and hLBD distributions supports conservation of negative cooperativity.

results.result: NMR titration experiments demonstrate that LC8 preferentially binds to C-terminal motifs (QT4-7) of dLBD over N-terminal motifs (QT1-3), with all sites showing some occupancy even at low LC8 ratios. The QT3 TMT motif is confirmed as a functional LC8 binding site. Motif environment rather than local sequence determines binding affinity.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C96 use NMR peak intensity changes to map LC8 binding preferences. The data show faster peak attenuation for QT4-7 than QT1-3, consistent with ITC showing QT4-6 has highest affinity. The QT4 motif shows different binding kinetics in QT2-4 versus QT4-6 constructs, supporting context-dependence. The observation that all peaks attenuate even at low LC8 ratios supports an ensemble model. NMR dynamics data (C96) provide a mechanistic explanation for C-terminal preference.

results.result: Cell-based luciferase reporter assays demonstrate that ASCIZ transcriptional activity is inversely correlated with LC8 binding affinity. Mutants with fewer LC8 binding sites show higher transcriptional activity, with AAA1-4,8-11 (3 sites, Kd=4.4 μM) showing 2.5x activity of WT, while AAA8-11 (7 sites, Kd=0.7 μM) shows activity equal to or lower than WT.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C107 provide functional validation of the biophysical findings. The inverse correlation between LC8 affinity and transcriptional activity is demonstrated across multiple mutants with statistical significance (p<0.01). The trend is clear despite small differences between constructs. The AAA-all exception (C104-C105) is acknowledged and a plausible explanation offered (dimerization requirement). The data support the model that LC8 occupancy tunes transcriptional activity.

results.result: ASCIZ forms a dynamic ensemble of complexes with LC8 where transcriptional activity is inversely proportional to LC8 occupancy. Low occupancy complexes are proposed to maintain basal LC8 transcription levels, acting as a buffer that allows LC8 concentration changes without dramatic transcriptional shifts, which is important for cellular homeostasis.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C5 and C108-C110 present the integrated model supported by the biophysical and cellular data. The inverse relationship between LC8 occupancy and transcriptional activity is demonstrated experimentally (C3, C100-C103). The preference for low occupancy complexes at saturating LC8 is shown by multiple techniques (C4, C64-C77). The buffering model (C108-C110) is a reasonable inference from the data, though it remains a proposed mechanism requiring further validation.

results.result: Human ASCIZ contains 11 functional LC8 binding sites, the highest number of any LC8 partner protein identified to date. This enrichment in LC8-binding sites is conserved throughout the animal kingdom.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C27-C29 establish ASCIZ as unique among LC8 partners. C27 cites published work identifying 11 sites in human ASCIZ. C28 compares to other known partners (Nup159 has 5, others have 3). C29 shows conservation across species in Figure 1d. The claims are well-supported by both current data and literature.

results.result: ASCIZ-LC8 interactions exhibit both positive cooperativity (first 2-4 motifs) and negative cooperativity (regulating higher-order assemblies). When LC8 concentration exceeds buffering capacity, fully occupied complexes form to switch off transcription.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C116 synthesize the cooperativity findings. Positive cooperativity is demonstrated by ITC (C63, C114). Negative cooperativity is shown by dominance of low occupancy complexes at saturation (C68, C115). The switching mechanism (C116) is a reasonable inference from the transcription data showing lowest activity with highest occupancy, though it remains somewhat speculative.

results.result: Comparison with Nup159 reveals that ASCIZ:LC8 complexes are more dynamic and heterogeneous despite similar overall affinity. This difference may reflect functional requirements for transcriptional autoregulation versus nuclear pore assembly.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C120 provide important context by comparing ASCIZ to another multivalent LC8 partner. The EM data clearly show Nup159 forms stable, uniform complexes while ASCIZ forms sparse, heterogeneous structures (C78-C79). The similar affinities (2.9 vs 0.9 μM) make the structural difference more striking. The functional interpretation (C120) is speculative but reasonable.

results.result: ASCIZ knockout phenotypes in mice and Drosophila are severe and are rescued by LC8 overexpression, demonstrating that ASCIZ's primary function is regulation of LC8 expression. LC8 conditional knockout phenotypes closely match ASCIZ knockout phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C13 establish the biological importance of ASCIZ-LC8 regulation through cited literature. The rescue experiments (C11) and phenocopy by LC8 knockout (C13) provide strong evidence that ASCIZ's main function is LC8 regulation. All claims are properly attributed to published work.

results.result: LC8 is a conserved homodimeric hub protein that binds to intrinsically disordered motifs containing TQT residues, creating an IDP duplex scaffold that facilitates higher-order assembly. LC8 has over 40 characterized partners with dozens more predicted.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C26 provide essential background on LC8 structure and function, all properly cited from literature. The structural details (C14, C17-C20, C22) are well-established. The hub protein concept (C16, C25-C26) provides context for why LC8 regulation is important. These are foundational claims supporting the significance of the work.

results.result: ASCIZ regulates LC8 transcription through negative autoregulation. Disruption of ASCIZ-LC8 binding increases LC8 transcription while LC8 overexpression decreases it. Regulation of LC8 levels is critical for cellular health as LC8 expression varies among tissues and its overexpression affects cancer cell proliferation.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C36 establish the regulatory relationship and its importance, citing published work. The negative autoregulation (C30-C32) is demonstrated in prior studies. The hypothesis that ASCIZ acts as an LC8 sensor (C33) is appropriately labeled as such. The importance for cellular health (C34-C36) is supported by cited tissue-specific expression and cancer studies.

results.result: Human ASCIZ contains an exceptionally long intrinsically disordered domain (600 amino acids, 73% of sequence). IDRs longer than 50 amino acids are considered significant for transcription factors, and IDR length can control transcriptional activity through energetic frustration.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C113 contextualize ASCIZ's structural features. C111 is a straightforward calculation from sequence. C112-C113 cite literature establishing the significance of long IDRs in transcription factors. These claims support the novelty of ASCIZ as a model system.

results.result: Other transcription factors like Ets-1 and p53 are regulated by multisite modifications. Ets-1 phosphorylation inhibits DNA binding ~20-fold, while p53 has over 50 interdependent modifications that modulate binding to regulatory proteins in a phosphorylation-dependent manner.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C124 provide comparative context from literature on other multivalent transcription factors. All claims are properly cited. These examples establish that multisite regulation is common, making ASCIZ's mechanism of binding multiple copies of its gene product novel by comparison.

results.result: ASCIZ forms puncta in cell culture in response to DNA damage (MMS treatment), and these puncta do not form without LC8, indicating that LC8 binding to multiple motifs is necessary for foci formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C126 cite published observations of ASCIZ puncta formation. The LC8-dependence (C126) is an inference from cited work. This provides additional functional context for multivalent LC8 binding, though it's not directly investigated in this study.

results.result: The prevalence of intrinsic disorder and multivalency among transcription factors suggests that formation of heterogeneous, dynamic complexes is a widespread mechanism for tuning transcriptional regulation.
results.evaluation: Claim C6 is explicitly speculative, extrapolating from ASCIZ to transcription factors generally. While the prevalence of disorder and multivalency in transcription factors is established (cited), the conclusion that dynamic complex formation is widespread is not demonstrated. This is a reasonable hypothesis for future work but lacks direct evidence beyond the ASCIZ system studied here.
